lesson.title: QUIC: Rebuilding Transport on Top of UDP
lesson.summary: QUIC is a modern transport protocol, standardized in an IETF RFC and built on top of UDP, that eliminates TCP's head-of-line blocking across streams and folds connection setup and encryption into a single fast handshake.
lesson.body:
Every mechanism covered so far, congestion control, fast retransmit, retransmission timers, SACK, is part of TCP, and TCP has been extraordinarily successful for decades. But TCP has two structural properties that became harder to live with as the web evolved toward pages loading dozens of resources over a single connection. First, TCP delivers bytes to the application in strict sequential order: if one segment is lost, every byte after it, even bytes belonging to logically unrelated data multiplexed on the same connection, must wait until that lost segment is recovered before any of it can be delivered upward. This is head-of-line blocking, and it becomes a real cost when protocols like HTTP/2 multiplex many independent request-response streams over a single TCP connection: a single lost packet stalls every stream, not just the one whose data it happened to carry. Second, establishing a new secure TCP connection requires a TCP handshake followed by a separate TLS handshake, each costing at least one round trip, so a fresh HTTPS connection typically needs two or three round trips of pure setup before any application data moves at all.

QUIC is a transport protocol designed to fix both problems, and it takes an unusual approach to deployment: rather than being implemented as a new protocol directly on top of IP the way TCP and UDP are, QUIC is built on top of UDP. This is a deliberate, pragmatic choice. Decades of middleboxes, firewalls, NAT devices, and operating system network stacks across the internet are tuned to recognize and handle TCP and UDP specifically, and getting a genuinely new IP-layer protocol deployed globally has proven extremely difficult in practice, since many devices along real paths simply drop anything unfamiliar. UDP, by contrast, is close to universally passed through. QUIC exploits this by riding inside UDP datagrams while implementing its own reliability, ordering, and congestion control entirely in software above UDP, effectively using UDP as a thin, widely-tolerated shim rather than as a transport in its own right. QUIC's design and wire format are specified in RFC 9000, published by the IETF, making it, like TCP before it, a protocol defined through the formal RFC process rather than a private or proprietary specification.

To solve head-of-line blocking, QUIC multiplexes multiple independent streams within a single connection at the transport layer itself, rather than layering multiplexing on top of a single ordered byte stream the way HTTP/2 does on top of TCP. Because QUIC understands stream boundaries natively, a lost packet carrying data for one stream only blocks delivery of that stream; other streams whose data arrived intact continue to be delivered to the application without waiting. This directly targets the exact problem that made HTTP/2 over TCP disappointing on lossy connections, such as many mobile networks.

To solve slow connection setup, QUIC combines the transport handshake and the cryptographic handshake into a single exchange, using TLS 1.3 integrated directly into QUIC's own handshake rather than layered as a separate protocol on top of an already-established connection. A new QUIC connection can typically begin sending encrypted application data after just one round trip, and a client reconnecting to a server it has recently talked to can often send application data immediately in its very first flight, called zero round trip time, or 0-RTT, resumption. QUIC connections are also identified by a connection ID rather than by the traditional four-tuple of source and destination IP address and port that TCP relies on, which allows a QUIC connection to survive a client's network change, moving from Wi-Fi to cellular data, for instance, without tearing down and re-establishing the connection, something a TCP connection generally cannot do since changing IP address breaks the identifying tuple. QUIC is the transport underneath HTTP/3, and its arrival represents the most significant rethinking of internet transport protocol design since TCP and UDP themselves were defined, built by taking the lessons learned from decades of TCP congestion control, retransmission timing, and acknowledgment strategy covered throughout this unit, and reimplementing them, encrypted and stream-aware from the ground up, on top of the one lower-layer protocol the internet was actually willing to let through.
